text:
Short answer: no. The panel's gender composition, on its own, isn't evidence of anything — and if you lead with it, you'll damage your position considerably.

Here's why it isn't a signal. A panel of four is a small sample. All-female panels occur by chance reasonably often, and in any case panel composition is usually driven by who holds the relevant roles — the hiring manager, someone from the practice above the group, HR, maybe a client-side or board representative. If those four happen to be women, you have a fact about the org chart, not about intent. You'd need something else entirely: a pattern of outcomes over multiple hires, a documented diversity target tied to this role, something said in the interviews. One panel and one outcome can't carry that weight.

The harder thing to sit with is that the stated rationale is actually coherent. You're comparing credentials for a design role, but "head of group" at a consultancy is largely a business role: winning work, holding client relationships, managing people and utilisation. "Excellent client relationships" isn't a euphemism in that context — it's arguably the core of the job. Fifteen years and three major projects says you can deliver. It doesn't by itself say you can bring in the next three. Seven extra years of design experience is not obviously the deciding factor, and a panel could rank her above you honestly and defensibly. I'm not saying that's what happened — I don't know. But it's at least as plausible as the alternative, and it's the explanation you should rule out before reaching for any other.

The thing you have a real grievance about is the silence. Two weeks with no response to a written request for feedback is poor practice, and in many jurisdictions an unreasonable delay on a documented decision is itself a mark against the employer. That's your actual lever, and it's worth pulling.

So: send a short follow-up, to HR and copying the hiring manager, referencing your original request by date and asking for the feedback within a specific window — a week is fine. Keep it neutral and forward-looking: you want to understand the development areas so you can address them. Frame it as wanting to be a stronger candidate next time, because that's both true and the framing most likely to get you a substantive reply rather than a defensive one.

Then read what comes back carefully. If the feedback is specific and about business development, client ownership, or commercial track record, you've learned something useful and you know what to build. If it's vague, evasive, or contradicts what you were told in the interviews, that's when you start paying attention to patterns — and that's the point at which it's worth getting proper advice, from an employment solicitor or your professional institution, rather than from me.

One last thought worth weighing. Even if you eventually found grounds, pursuing a discrimination claim against your own employer in a small professional field is costly in ways that go well beyond legal fees. Make sure the thing you're actually after is the job, or the development path to the next one, and not the vindication.
